belief: Something terrible is going to happen.
origins: A sense of coming doom often follows a sudden shock, such as an unexpected death, diagnosis, or accident, which teaches the mind that disaster can strike without warning. It can also grow in homes where parents were constantly worried, or where something bad really did happen often. Worry can feel like protection, as if expecting the worst could prevent it.
teaches: Jesus told His followers not to worry about tomorrow, because each day has enough trouble of its own. Paul urged believers to bring every anxious thought to God in prayer with thanksgiving, and promised that God’s peace would guard their hearts and minds. The psalmist describes a person who does not fear bad news because his heart is steady, trusting in the Lord. Worry cannot add a single hour to life. God does not ask us to pretend bad things never happen; He asks us to trust Him with tomorrow.
self_statements: I just know something bad is coming.
If I stop worrying, it will happen.
Every phone call might be bad news.
Things are too good; something will go wrong.
I need to be prepared for the worst.
I can’t shake this feeling of dread.
errors: Jumping from a small worry to the worst possible outcome.
Believing danger is coming because I feel dread.
Believing my worry somehow prevents bad things.
questions: What evidence do I have that something terrible is about to happen?
How many times have I felt this dread and nothing happened?
Does my worrying actually prevent anything?
If something hard did happen, how might God help me through it?
What does Jesus say about tomorrow?
What can I do today instead of worrying about tomorrow?
truth: Hard things can happen, and I cannot prevent every one. But this feeling of dread is not a prophecy, and worry does not protect me. God holds tomorrow. I can bring my fears to Him, live today, and trust Him to help me with whatever comes.
hw_truths: Tomorrow will take care of itself.
God’s peace can guard my heart and mind.
Dread is a feeling, not a prediction.
Worry cannot add an hour to my life.
log: Each day, write down any fear about something terrible happening. A week later, note whether it happened.
actions: Keep a list of the bad things you predict for two weeks. At the end, count how many actually happened.
Give yourself 15 minutes a day to write worries and pray over them. Outside that time, gently postpone worry.
When dread rises, pray Philippians 4:6–7 aloud, naming each fear and thanking God for one thing.
If dread is constant or comes with panic attacks, talk with a doctor or counselor.
tracker: A fear that did not come true
prayer: Lord, I am so often afraid that something terrible is coming. Thank You that You hold tomorrow. I give You my fears today. Guard my heart and mind with Your peace, and help me live this day with You. Amen.
